categories.heading: A. Core concepts
categories.descriptionHtml: These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.

entries.title: Ethotechnics
entries.bodyHtml:
Ethotechnics is the engineering discipline concerned with keeping authority, evidence, capability, consequence, and correction coupled tightly enough that increasing machine agency does not silently become unreviewable institutional power.

Its unit of governance is the consequential decision and the delegated agency that produced it, and its working question is whether that delegation is still a justified delegation today. The method states the chain, the six state variables, and the twelve laws that the standards bind.
examples: A hospital release board requires consent checks, stop controls, and named repair owners before deploying triage updates.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: Documentation maps moral obligations to concrete mechanisms (stoppability, contestability, repair ownership).
Teams can show a shipped feature where moral performance was designed, measured, and iterated.
entries.genealogy: Draws from ethics, safety engineering, and systems design to align governance, product, and operations around observable moral performance.

entries.title: Moral Behavior (of Systems)
entries.bodyHtml: Observable system outcomes that prevent harm, distribute burden fairly, and keep people able to contest and recover. Moral behavior is evaluated via MPIs like time-to-halt, reversibility, and fair burden distribution—not by stated intent. A system does not “behave morally” if MPIs are tracked but do not trigger pause rules, remediation, or resourcing.
examples: A payments platform slows risky recommendations, surfaces a human review queue, and documents reversals when fraud indicators spike.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: MPIs are tracked and drive operational thresholds or pause rules.
Post-incident reviews tie outcomes to system controls rather than intent statements.
entries.genealogy: Defines the observable outcomes Ethotechnics expects across governance, design, and operations.

entries.title: Ethical Load Path
entries.bodyHtml: The traceable chain of authority, decisions, and controls that carries moral responsibility through a system. A clear ethical load path names who can stop, reverse, or repair harm at each stage, linking design authority, oversight horizons, and the repair log so handoffs remain accountable.
examples: A transit authority publishes a named escalation map for halting automated dispatch, including after-hours owners.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: Each lifecycle stage has a named owner with authority to stop, reverse, or repair, plus backup coverage.
Incident reviews show the escalation path was used without dead ends or orphaned decisions.
entries.genealogy: Adapts engineering load paths to accountability so responsibility stays traceable across handoffs.

entries.title: Ethotechnic Audit
entries.bodyHtml: A structured assessment of a system’s moral capabilities, including stoppability, reversibility, burden distribution, contestability, and accountability. Ethotechnic audits validate evidence, stress-test pathways, and define remediation steps with named owners.
examples: After a harmful rollout, a platform audit verifies stop controls, reversal paths, and repair ownership before relaunch.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: Audit evidence includes drills, logs, and user-facing pathways for contesting and repairing harm.
Remediation plans are time-bound, assigned to owners, and re-audited after major changes.
entries.genealogy: Builds on safety and compliance audits while centering harm prevention, repair, and accountability.

entries.title: Conviviality
entries.bodyHtml: The degree to which tools and institutions expand people’s agency, cooperation, and right of refusal instead of enclosing them. Convivial systems keep permission surfaces wide, make opting out safe, and let communities shape the service.
examples: A mutual aid platform lets neighbors pause notifications or change delivery preferences without losing access to support.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: People can refuse or change terms without losing core access or being penalized.
Interfaces surface shared control settings instead of only provider defaults.
entries.genealogy: Extends human-centered design by insisting that agency and refusal remain durable at scale.

entries.title: Ethotechnic Maturity
entries.bodyHtml: A developmental scale describing how consistently a system embodies Ethotechnic capabilities across its lifecycle. Early maturity focuses on stopping acute harms; later stages add graceful degradation, contestability, and routine care retrospectives. Mature systems publish SLJs, maintain repair capacity, and review moral performance on a steady cadence.
examples: A rail operator publishes service-level justice metrics, runs quarterly pause drills, and funds dedicated repair staffing.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: A maturity level is documented with evidence for each capability and reviewed after major releases.
Maintenance and repair staffing, budgets, and tools are recurring, not ad hoc.
entries.genealogy: Adapts maturity modeling into a roadmap for moral performance and sustained care.

entries.title: Legibility
entries.bodyHtml: How understandable a system’s actions, reasoning, and ownership are to the people affected by it. Legibility complements explainability for accountability and transparent design authority so people can find who decided, why, and how to respond. Legibility is discoverability of who/why/what-next; it does not guarantee the system can be changed.
examples: Residents receive a plain-language notice that names the office, rule, and appeal path behind a zoning decision.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: Decision notices include a plain-language rationale, owner, and next step for contesting.
Affected people can reach the policy basis and escalation path within a single click or call.
entries.genealogy: Moves transparency from disclosure to actionable understanding for the people impacted.

entries.title: Sociotechnical Alignment
entries.bodyHtml: Alignment achieved not just in the model, but across tools, interfaces, incentives, workflows, and organizational structures. Sociotechnical alignment keeps the ethical load path intact under pressure.
examples: Policy, tooling, and incentives all enforce the same stoppability rules.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: Incentives and KPIs reinforce, rather than undermine, moral requirements.
Incident reviews can trace breakdowns between policy intent and operational tooling.
entries.genealogy: Bridges organizational design and system behavior to keep moral intent durable.

entries.title: Delegated Agency
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to act with consequence on an institution's behalf, held by a machine, a human, or an assembly of both. Delegated agency is created by an authority grant and exercised through a decision system; it is not a property of the model that happens to be running.

It matters because agency is the quantity that accumulates. An institution that tracks capability but not delegated agency cannot say how much of its consequential action it has handed over, or whether it still holds the correction capacity to take any of it back.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: The institution can list, for one workflow, every action class a machine may take on its behalf.
Each listed action class traces to a named grant holder rather than to a team or a system name.
Growth in delegated action classes over a quarter is reported alongside growth in correction capacity.
entries.genealogy: Names the object the twelve laws govern: not the model, but the agency an institution has handed to it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A register of action classes a machine may perform on the institution's behalf, with holders.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A new action class appearing only after an authorization decision, visible in the register history.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of authorized action classes per workflow, tracked against correction capacity over time.

entries.title: Consequential Decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A decision that changes someone's access, money, obligations, safety, or standing, and that the institution would have to answer for. The consequential decision is the unit of governance in Ethotechnics: each one is a link in the chain from evidence to authority to consequence to correction.

Naming the unit matters because it fixes where the governance load sits. Systems governed at the level of the model leave the decisions themselves unaccounted for, which is where unowned harm collects and where prospective auditability has to be designed in.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: The system declares which of its outputs are consequential decisions and which are not.
Each consequential decision emits a record naming the evidence, the grant, and the responsible holder.
A person affected by one can obtain that record without filing a formal request.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics takes the consequential decision, rather than the model or the product, as the unit that standards, mechanisms, and evals attach to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A decision record schema listing evidence refs, grant id, holder, and consequence class.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A decision reconstructed months later from its record alone, without asking the team.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions that emit a complete record, sampled monthly.

entries.title: Decision System
entries.bodyHtml:
The assembled machinery that produces a consequential decision: models, rules engines, queues, humans, policies, and the data they read. Ethotechnics governs the decision system rather than any one component, because the same substrate-independent questions apply whichever part made the call, and the deployment is classified by its substrate profile rather than by which component is fashionable.

It matters because component-level assurance does not compose. A verified model inside an unaudited decision system still produces decisions no one can reconstruct, which is why assurance is tagged with the evaluation layer it actually holds at, and why reconstructing a past decision depends on prospective auditability designed into the system.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: A diagram names every component that can alter a decision, including humans and lookup tables.
Assurance claims state which component they cover and which they do not.
Changing any component triggers review of the decision system, not only of that component.
entries.genealogy: Generalizes the agent safety object model so that a rules engine, a human reviewer, and a model are governed by the same primitives.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A component inventory for one decision path, with the alteration each component can make.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An assurance claim rejected for covering a component rather than the decision system.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision paths with a current component inventory.

entries.title: Justified Delegation
entries.bodyHtml:
A delegation whose authority, evidence, and correction capacity are all currently in force: the grant sits in an allowed grant state, the policy record it rests on has not expired, and the institution can still meet its correction obligation. Justification is a present-tense property, not a fact about the launch review.

It matters because most delegations fail by outliving their justification rather than by being wrong at the start. Asking whether a delegation is justified today is the operational form of treating authority as an authority lease.
entries.scope: A. Core concepts. These terms define the Ethotechnics discipline itself and set expectations for moral system design.
operationalTests: For any decision, the institution can show the grant was in an allowed state at the time it was made.
Every grant names the policy records it depends on, and each has an unexpired validity date.
A grant whose evidence basis has lapsed cannot authorize action until it is renewed.
entries.genealogy: Compresses Laws II and III into a single testable question about the present state of a delegation rather than the quality of its original approval.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant record with state, evidence basis, expiry, and renewal basis fields populated.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An action refused because the grant authorizing it had lapsed into review_required.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions taken under a grant that was in an allowed state.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target 100 percent; any exception is an incident.

examples: A claims triage delegation is suspended automatically when the population-drift policy record passes its review date, and resumes only after a fresh drift study is filed.

categories.descriptionHtml: Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.

entries.title: Moral Latency
entries.bodyHtml: The lag between harm occurring and the system detecting or responding to it. Automation can scale impact faster than oversight, so moral latency demands velocity friction and ethical interrupts that shrink response time.
examples: A clinic triage chatbot keeps routing patients while harm reports queue for hours, delaying escalation.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Time-to-detect harm exceeds time-to-scale the impact.
Alerts are not tied to pause, rollback, or escalation controls for moral risk.
entries.genealogy: Applies latency thinking to harm detection so response windows stay tight.

entries.title: Accountability Diffusion
entries.bodyHtml: Responsibility spreads across teams, vendors, and incentives until no one can intervene. Accountability diffusion erodes design authority and leaves harm without a decisive owner. If no one can unilaterally stop or reverse the harm, accountability is diffused.
examples: A support ticket bounces between a vendor and a hospital compliance team with no one empowered to pause the rollout.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Escalation maps lack a single owner with authority to stop or repair.
Incident reviews show repeated handoffs without a clear decision point.
entries.genealogy: Names the structural cause of unowned harm in complex institutions and supply chains.

entries.title: Extraction
entries.bodyHtml: When a system pulls value—data, attention, labor, or social capital—without returning care, consent, or repair. Extraction hides true costs through externalization and steep burden gradients, hollowing trust.
examples: A data-labeling program offloads unpaid overnight verification to gig workers while the platform reports clean metrics.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Value metrics are tracked without corresponding burden or consent metrics.
Unpaid or unacknowledged labor is required to keep the system functioning.
entries.genealogy: Frames value capture as a moral risk, not just an economic one.

entries.title: Extraction by Endurance
entries.bodyHtml: Systems that rely on workers or users absorbing fragility through burnout, emotional labor, or unpaid cognitive work—often mislabeled as “resilience.” Ethotechnic practice aims to invert this burden with fair burden distribution.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Sustained service quality depends on overtime, heroics, or unpaid labor.
Reported stability drops when people stop compensating for failures.
entries.genealogy: Calls out resilience narratives that mask structural fragility.

entries.title: Drift (System Drift)
entries.bodyHtml: The tendency of systems to drift toward harm over time when incentives, data, or constraints shift. Without protective friction and moral performance indicators, drift quietly erodes safeguards and accountability.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Performance metrics improve while harm or complaints trend upward.
Controls are not reviewed when data, vendors, or policies change.
entries.genealogy: Warns that stability requires ongoing recalibration as systems evolve.

entries.title: Externalization
entries.bodyHtml:
Pushing risk, cost, or harm onto other teams, communities, or the future so internal metrics look clean. Externalization appears as pollution, shadow labor, or brittle dependencies outside audits.

Ethotechnics counters it with oversight horizons, MPIs, and transparent repair logs.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Costs show up in downstream teams without corresponding resources or ownership.
Audits exclude dependencies where harms are reported.
entries.genealogy: Names the gap between local optimization and systemic responsibility.

entries.title: Brittleness
entries.bodyHtml: When a system fractures under real-world variance—unexpected inputs, refusals, or edge cases—forcing humans to absorb the impact. Brittleness signals missing soft edges, thin graceful degradation, and poor refusal tolerance.
examples: A flight booking bot fails on hyphenated surnames, forcing agents to rebook travelers at the counter.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Small input variance triggers hard failures instead of safe fallbacks.
Human operators routinely patch failures without tooling support or documented playbooks.
entries.genealogy: Highlights the need for soft edges, graceful degradation, and refusal tolerance.

entries.title: Optimization Myopia
entries.bodyHtml: Metric chasing that narrows attention to throughput or growth while ignoring MPIs. Myopic optimization erodes contestability, raises failure load, and often fuels extraction.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Success metrics improve while contestability or reversibility degrades.
Teams cannot articulate the moral tradeoffs behind optimizations or track MPIs.
entries.genealogy: Warns against single-metric tuning that crowds out moral performance.

entries.title: Precision Laundering
entries.bodyHtml: Using detailed metrics or probabilistic scores to disguise inequity as objectivity. Precision laundering hides burden gradients and externalization behind statistical gloss, undermining explainability for accountability and meaningful contestation.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: High-confidence scores are presented without error bounds, provenance, or contestability paths.
Appeals are dismissed because numeric outputs are treated as unquestionable despite uneven impacts.
entries.genealogy: Calls out false certainty in quantified systems and the misuse of precision as legitimacy.

entries.title: Compliance Collapse
entries.bodyHtml: When rigid policy checklists replace judgment, causing teams to follow rules while harm worsens. Compliance collapse occurs when design authority is weak and contestability is low, leaving no path to pause or repair.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Teams meet checklist requirements but still cannot stop or reverse harm.
Escalations stall because procedures lack discretionary authority or override lanes.
entries.genealogy: Warns when compliance becomes a substitute for care and accountability.

entries.title: Ethics Debt
entries.bodyHtml: The accumulation of unresolved ethical risk from shipping capabilities faster than governance, ownership, and repair mechanisms. Ethics debt grows when maintenance debt outpaces the repair log and risks remain unfunded.
examples: A recommender launches without consent review, adding unresolved risks to the repair log backlog.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Open ethical risks outnumber resourced remediation plans and owners.
New launches add obligations without increasing repair capacity or budget.
entries.genealogy: Frames ethical risk as a backlog that compounds without investment.

entries.title: Unowned Harm
entries.bodyHtml: Negative outcomes for which no clear individual or role is accountable, even though the system caused them. Unowned harm signals accountability diffusion and weak traceable ownership.
examples: Denied applicants cannot identify a responsible team to contest a decision or request reversal.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Affected people cannot find a named owner or appeal path within the product.
Incident reviews conclude with no accountable role assigned or funded repair.
entries.genealogy: Names the moral gap created when accountability is absent.

entries.title: Capability Overhang
entries.bodyHtml: When a system’s power exceeds the maturity of its controls, making failures likely even without malicious intent. Capability overhang shows up as strong automation but weak stoppability or reversibility.
examples: A model can auto-approve loans, but rollback and auditing are manual and slow.

Teams can point to a concrete example that demonstrates capability overhang in practice.

entries.title: Ethics Theater
entries.bodyHtml: Public displays of ethical concern without operational mechanisms that change system behavior. Ethics theater often masks compliance collapse and low contestability.
examples: The team publishes a code of ethics but lacks monitoring or a repair log.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Ethics artifacts exist, but there are no operational stop, contest, or repair mechanisms behind them.
Incident reviews surface policy language without evidence of real-world enforcement.

entries.title: Authority Drift
entries.bodyHtml:
The gap that opens when what a system actually does moves away from what its authority grant permits or what its evidence supports. Drift arrives through added integrations, widened inputs, quietly raised thresholds, and habits that outlive the exception that created them, and it accumulates through the automation ratchet.

It matters because every individual step looks too small to review. Drift is detected by comparing observed action classes from capability discovery against grant scope, and it is what justified delegation and the authority lease exist to catch.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Observed action classes are reconciled against grant scope on a stated cadence.
Exceptions granted during incidents carry an expiry and are reconciled after the incident closes.
A widening that no one authorized appears in the reconciliation report rather than in a postmortem.
entries.genealogy: Names the drift Laws I, II, and XI describe, in the form an auditor can measure: observed behavior minus authorized scope.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reconciliation report listing observed action classes not covered by any live grant.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An unauthorized integration disabled after appearing in reconciliation.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of ungrounded action classes per reconciliation cycle, trended.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target zero; any non-zero count opens a review.

entries.title: Automation Ratchet
entries.bodyHtml:
Scope growth by accretion, where each extension of an automated system is too small to trigger review and no single step is the one that widened the delegation. The ratchet turns one way only: successful operation is read as licence to extend.

It matters because the end state bears no relation to what was originally justified and no single decision can be pointed at. The countermeasure is to make each widening an expansion decision, which is also what keeps authority drift from being invisible.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Scope changes are logged against the grant, however small, with a cumulative view available.
A cumulative threshold exists that forces a full re-authorization regardless of step size.
Reviewers are shown the original justification alongside current scope, not only the delta.
entries.genealogy: Names the failure Law XI describes, where success is treated as authorization rather than as a reason for a new authorization decision.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A cumulative scope history per grant, showing every widening since first authorization.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A small extension refused because it crossed a cumulative re-authorization threshold.
minimumEvidence.metric: Scope delta since original authorization, per grant.

entries.title: Institutional Capture
entries.bodyHtml:
The state in which a system has absorbed enough of an institution's capability, staff, and decision paths that the institution can no longer meaningfully evaluate, constrain, or replace it. Capture is not vendor lock-in alone; it includes losing the internal expertise needed to judge the system's output.

It matters because a captured institution still runs its governance rituals and can no longer act on them. Capture is the terminal form of normalized dependence, and it is the reason preserved capacity is protected long before it is needed.

operationalTests: The institution can name who would evaluate the system's output if the vendor disappeared.

Governance decisions about the system are made by people who do not depend on it for their work.

entries.title: Rubber-Stamp Review
entries.bodyHtml:
Review that produces approvals at a rate and speed incompatible with actual scrutiny, usually because the reviewer lacks time, information, authority, or permission to disagree. The artifact of review exists; the control does not.

It matters because rubber-stamp review reads as compliance in every audit that counts approvals rather than reversals. It is the failure meaningful control tests for and the one an intervention specification is written to prevent.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Median review time is reported alongside approval rate for every review queue.
A reviewer can point to a recent case they altered or refused.
Review capacity is compared against decision volume rather than assumed adequate.
entries.genealogy: Names the practical failure of Law IX oversight: the human is present, on the record, and unable to change anything.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Review queue statistics showing volume, median review time, and outcome distribution.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A review queue throttled because time per case fell below the scrutiny floor.
minimumEvidence.metric: Approval rate and median seconds per review, reported together.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Investigate any queue with approval rate above 98 percent and median review under 30 seconds.

entries.title: Normalized Dependence
entries.bodyHtml:
The condition in which reliance on a system has become invisible because it is ordinary: no one records it, no fallback is maintained, and withdrawal is no longer a question anyone asks. This is institutional dependence, meaning what the institution has come to rely on, and it should not be confused with the record-level dependence in STD-07 Article III, which governs what a given record rests on.

It matters because normalized dependence is what makes dependency state hard to measure and institutional capture hard to notice until a correction is needed and turns out to be unavailable.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Common patterns where responsibility dissolves and harm accelerates.
operationalTests: Someone can state, without research, what happens to each dependent workflow if the system stops.
Fallbacks named in the dependency record have been exercised within a stated interval.
New dependents are recorded when they appear rather than discovered during an incident.
entries.genealogy: Names the everyday form of the Law V failure, where dependence is real, unrecorded, and therefore ungoverned.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A dependency record listing every dependent workflow and its maintained fallback.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A new dependent workflow appearing in the record at onboarding, not at incident time.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of dependent workflows with an exercised fallback.

entries.title: Stoppability
entries.bodyHtml:
A system's ability to halt harmful processes quickly, safely, and deliberately—without requiring heroism or escalation. Stoppability pairs ethical interrupts with measurable time-to-halt targets and clear operator authority.

Strong stoppability means stop paths are rehearsed, observable, and usable under stress—not hidden behind exceptional permissions.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Each high-risk workflow has documented stop controls, owners, and on-call coverage.
Time-to-halt targets are met during drills or real incidents, with outcomes logged.

entries.title: Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
Critical actions can be undone and people restored to a safe prior state. Damage is not permanent by default, and time-to-restore stays low.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.

operationalTests: Critical actions have tested rollback or remediation paths that restore data and access.
Time-to-restore targets are met during drills and documented in the repair log.

minimumEvidence.behavior: Reversal executed during drills or incidents with people restored to their prior state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time-to-restore targets tracked and met across reversal events.

entries.title: Fair Burden Distribution
entries.bodyHtml:
Failures should not fall hardest on the most vulnerable. Fair burden distribution treats time, cost, stress, and procedural labor as design variables and tracks them with measures like the user burden ratio.

When burden concentrates on people with the least capacity to absorb it, systems must rebalance defaults, staffing, and escalation pathways.

entries.title: Contestability
entries.bodyHtml:
People affected by system decisions can challenge, change, or overturn them, and win. Contestability requires a visible permission surface and a healthy appeal passage rate.

It has four parts and needs all four: standing, meaning a named party may raise the challenge; a channel that receives it; an obliged responder who must answer on a clock against a stated standard; and a state change the challenge is capable of producing. Three of the four is a complaints process. The apparatus that supplies them is a standing mechanism, and the fourth part is what gives a challenge procedural force rather than a reply.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Appeals route to empowered reviewers with authority to overturn outcomes.
Appeal passage rate and response time are tracked and used to improve decisions.
Appeal outcomes include overturns, restorations, and policy changes—not just “review completed.”
Floor: if appeal passage rate stays below 5% for 30 days, trigger a forced redesign review.
Artifact requirement: Percentage of appeals that emit a decision artifact is tracked and published.

entries.bodyHtml: Explanations that are actionable, not decorative. They identify the decision owner, the data or policy basis, and how the outcome can be corrected, enabling contestability and audits. Explainability for accountability is legibility plus a working correction path.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Decision notices include the reason, data source, owner, and path to contest.

entries.title: Refusal-Tolerant Systems
entries.bodyHtml: The system remains usable when people opt out, are confused, make mistakes, or withdraw cooperation. Refusal tolerance prevents extraction by endurance by treating refusal as a valid input, not a failure state. Called “human” because it protects humans from being turned into the crumple zone when they refuse.

operationalTests: Opt-out or decline flows keep core services available without punitive delays.

entries.bodyHtml: Boundary conditions designed to cushion people instead of penalizing them—graduated responses, warnings before lockouts, and reversible defaults. Soft edges reduce failure load and guard against brittleness.

entries.bodyHtml: The ability to recognize failures as incidents (not anomalies) and respond with containment, logging, escalation, and repair. It pairs ethical interrupts with a living repair log.

entries.title: Capability Discovery
entries.bodyHtml:
The practice of finding out what an assembled decision system can actually do, including reachable tools, side effects, and action classes nobody intended to expose. Discovery is testing and cataloguing, and its output is a capability catalog rather than a permission.

It matters because capability that has not been discovered can be neither authorized nor refused. Keeping discovery separate from authorization is how a new capability stays outside the authority grant until someone decides it belongs there.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Discovery runs against the assembled system, including tools reachable through chained calls.
Discovery output is written to the catalog and never directly to a grant.
The harness confirms that a newly discovered capability is refused at execution until granted.
entries.genealogy: Operationalizes Law I by making discovery a first-class activity whose result is knowledge, not permission.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A discovery run report listing reachable action classes and how each was verified.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A discovered but ungranted capability refused at execution and logged.
minimumEvidence.metric: Interval since the last discovery run per decision system.

entries.title: Correction Capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
The measured ability to actually intervene: which interventions exist, who may invoke them, how long they take, and how much load the institution can absorb while they run. Capacity is counted in people, clocks, and rehearsals rather than asserted in a policy.

It matters because a correction obligation with no matching capacity is a promise the institution cannot keep. Capacity is the quantity that must grow alongside delegated agency, and it is the property an evaluation layer above the model is needed to test.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Every stated intervention has a named invoker, a measured time to effect, and a last-exercised date.
Capacity is compared against authority at each expansion review, not only at launch.
Interventions never exercised within a stated interval are treated as unproven.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law IV from a duty into a measurement: correction capacity is what the institution can demonstrate, not what it intends.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention inventory with invokers, time to effect, and last-exercised dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An intervention exercised in a drill within its stated time to effect.
minimumEvidence.metric: Ratio of authorized action volume to demonstrated correction throughput.

entries.title: Technical Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The first level of the reversibility ladder: the mechanism exists and works. The switch throws, the rollback completes, the state restores, and a test proves it on the version of the system currently running.

It matters as a floor rather than a finding. Technical reversibility is the cheapest of the three levels to claim and the least informative, because a working switch says nothing about whether operational reversibility or institutional reversibility would survive it being thrown.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: The rollback path is exercised against the current build, not a past one.
Restore completeness is measured, including derived state and downstream caches.
A failed rollback test blocks release rather than producing a follow-up ticket.
entries.genealogy: The first rung of the Law VI ladder, kept separate so a passing technical test cannot be reported as reversibility.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rollback test report against the current build, with restore completeness measured.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A rollback executed in a drill that restored state without manual repair.
minimumEvidence.metric: Rollback success rate and time to restore, per release.

entries.title: Operational Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The second level of the reversibility ladder: the people and processes can absorb the correction being made. Staff know the fallback, queues can hold the load, and the manual path has been exercised recently enough to work.

It matters because most corrections fail here rather than at the switch. Operational reversibility is what a withdrawal rehearsal measures, and its absence turns technical reversibility into a claim nobody will test during an incident.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: The fallback path has been run with real volume within a stated interval.
Staffing for the fallback is costed and available, not notional.
Backlog accumulated during a rehearsal is measured and shown to be recoverable.
entries.genealogy: The second rung of the Law VI ladder, where the question moves from the mechanism to the people who must live through its use.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rehearsal report showing the fallback carrying real work for a stated period.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Frontline staff executing the manual path without escalation during a drill.
minimumEvidence.metric: Backlog accumulated per hour of fallback operation, and time to clear it.

entries.title: Institutional Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The third level of the reversibility ladder: the organization can survive having made the correction. Commitments, contracts, reputations, and budgets all remain serviceable after withdrawal, which is the level beyond technical and operational reversibility.

It matters because a correction that would cause unacceptable damage will not be exercised, and an unexercisable correction is not a control. Institutional reversibility is the level that dependency state erodes and that preserved capacity is maintained to defend.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: The institutional consequences of withdrawal are written down, owned, and priced.
At least one senior owner can state what withdrawal would cost without preparing a paper.
Contracts and public commitments are reviewed for terms that make withdrawal unaffordable.
entries.genealogy: The third rung of the Law VI ladder and the level Law XII protects, since a system may draw on institutional capacity but may not consume it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A withdrawal impact assessment covering contracts, commitments, and budget.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A withdrawal decision taken and survived, or a rehearsal that priced it credibly.
minimumEvidence.metric: Estimated institutional cost of withdrawal, trended against exposure score.

entries.title: Intervention Specification
entries.bodyHtml:
The replacement for human in the loop as a control name. An intervention specification states who may intervene, on what signal, with what information, with authority over which state, on what timescale, and what happens when they disagree.

It matters because a role is not a control. Naming a human is compatible with that human being unable to alter anything, which is why oversight clauses resolve to an intervention specification and to meaningful control rather than to human override lanes alone, and why its absence shows up as rubber-stamp review.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: Each oversight clause resolves to a specification answering all six questions.
The specification names a state the human can alter, not only a decision they can approve.
A disagreement path exists and has been exercised at least once.
entries.genealogy: Retires human in the loop as a control name, per the vocabulary decision in the 2026-09 reconstruction plan, and gives Law IX a testable object.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention specification per oversight point, with signal, information, authority, and clock.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A human intervention that altered system state, traced end to end.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of oversight points with a complete specification, and interventions exercised per quarter.

entries.title: Prospective Auditability
entries.bodyHtml:
Designing a system so that the questions an audit will ask can be answered later, by recording evidence, authority, and reasoning at the time of each decision rather than reconstructing them afterwards. It is decided at build time and cannot be retrofitted onto decisions already made.

It matters because retrospective audits mostly discover that the record does not exist. Prospective auditability is what makes a consequential decision reviewable at all, and it is why a policy record is written before it is needed rather than assembled during an inquiry.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). Design requirements that keep people safe when systems scale.
operationalTests: The audit question set is written before launch and each question maps to a recorded field.
A sample decision from last quarter can be fully reconstructed from records alone.
Missing fields block release rather than becoming audit findings a year later.
entries.genealogy: Inverts the audit relationship: instead of auditing what was kept, the system keeps what will be audited.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An audit question set mapped to recorded fields, dated before launch.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A past decision reconstructed from records without contacting the owning team.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of audit questions answerable from records alone, sampled quarterly.

entries.title: Fail-Safe Mode
entries.bodyHtml:
The system defaults to the safest possible behavior when uncertain, prioritizing stoppability over throughput. In Ethotechnic practice, fail-safe mode is not a generic error page: it is a predesigned degraded state with bounded actions, clear status signals, and immediate escalation paths.

A fail-safe posture should preserve contestability and reduce irreversible harm while operators diagnose the incident.

entries.title: Grant State
entries.bodyHtml:
The current status of an authority grant, drawn from a closed set such as allowed, confirm_required, review_required, suspended, and withdrawn. Every action is checked against the state in force at the time it is taken, and every transition is recorded with its cause.

It matters because states are what triggers can move. Without an explicit grant state there is nothing for a review trigger to change, and monitoring stays decorative rather than governing.

entries.title: Capability Catalog
entries.bodyHtml:

It matters because the catalog is what an authority grant is written against. Comparing catalog to grants is the direct test of whether capability has outrun authority, and a catalog nobody refreshes silently stops being that test.

entries.title: Dependency State
entries.bodyHtml:

It matters because dependence quietly removes corrections from the menu. Tracked as a state, it can be scored through exposure score, read against the deployment's substrate profile, and countered by replenishing institutional reversibility.

entries.title: Substrate Profile

entries.title: Exposure Score

A composite indicator of how much structural risk a dependence carries, defined as dependency depth multiplied by substitution cost multiplied by correction latency. entries.bodyHtml: Cases do not become orphaned across handoffs; ownership persists through vacations, organizational changes, or vendor transfers. Case ownership continuity strengthens traceable ownership for contested decisions.

entries.title: Revisable Delegation
entries.bodyHtml:
Delegation of consequential work to a machine that stays tied to the evidence and beliefs that justified it, so the grant can be narrowed, suspended, or withdrawn when those change. A revisable delegation names its holder, its ceiling, what it depends on, and what would revoke it; an unrevisable one is a transfer with a delegation's name.

The question it serves is how an institution can become more capable without becoming less revisable. The record shape is defined in STD-07. The test is whether the institution can answer, for any past action, what it believed at the time, what it had authorized, and what has since changed.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every authorization record lists its revocation conditions and the beliefs it depends on.
A discrepancy that matches a revocation condition produces a revision within a declared clock.
Someone outside the system has standing to object, and the objection is answered on the record.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics uses Revisable Delegation to name the property that bounded autonomy, decision reversal authority, and meta-contestability jointly protect once an institution lets machines act on its behalf.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authorization record carrying holder, ceiling, depends_on, and revocation conditions.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A delegation narrowed or withdrawn in response to a recorded discrepancy, with the chain visible.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time from a matching discrepancy to the revision that answers it, against the declared clock.

examples: An agent's standing deploy permission is tied to a verified staging check; when the check breaks, the permission drops to confirm-mode automatically and the log shows which record forced it.

entries.title: Authority Grant
entries.bodyHtml:
The record that permits a named holder to take a bounded class of actions, for whom, under what conditions, and until when. A grant carries its scope, its evidence basis, its grant state, its expiry, and the policy records it depends on.

It matters because authority that is not written as a record cannot be reviewed, narrowed, or withdrawn. The grant is what makes authority drift detectable rather than merely regrettable after the fact.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every action class a system may perform maps to exactly one grant with a named holder.
Each grant states an expiry and the conditions under which it is revoked.
A grant with no revocation conditions is flagged as a transfer rather than a delegation.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics separates the grant from the capability so that Law I, capability does not imply authority, has an object to bind to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authority grant register with holder, scope, state, evidence basis, and expiry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An attempted action outside grant scope refused and logged with the grant id.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of live grants and share carrying a non-null expiry.

entries.title: Authority Lease
entries.bodyHtml:
The stance that a grant of authority is held for a term against a renewable justification rather than owned outright. A lease expires by default, and continuing an authority grant requires fresh evidence rather than the absence of complaints.

It matters because silence is the most common renewal mechanism in practice. Treating authority as a lease forces justified delegation to be re-established on a clock, and it puts the burden of proof on the delegation rather than on the people questioning it.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every grant has a renewal date, and passing it changes the grant state without human action.
Renewal packets cite new evidence, not the original approval.
The renewal burden rises with the consequence class and the elapsed duration of the grant.
entries.genealogy: States Law II as a property relationship: authority is leasehold, and absence of observed failure is not payment of the rent.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A renewal record naming the evidence that justifies continuing the grant for a further term.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant lapsing on its renewal date because no renewal packet was filed.
minimumEvidence.metric: Median age of live grants against their declared renewal interval.

entries.title: Policy Record
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned statement of the propositions a delegation rests on: what the model does, who the population is, what the downstream process catches, and when each claim expires. Grants cite policy records rather than restating their assumptions, which is what policy as state requires.

It matters because assumptions decay silently when they are held as launch documents. Held as a record with a version and an expiry, a policy can raise a review trigger and move a grant state when the world changes.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each policy record states its assumptions, its evidence, its version, and its review date.
Grants reference policy records by id and version rather than paraphrasing them.
Passing a review date changes the record status and propagates to every grant that cites it.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object: the propositions that justify a grant are stored where a change in the world can reach them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record with assumptions, evidence refs, version, and review date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A lapsed policy record moving its dependent grants to review_required.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose cited policy records are all within their review dates.

entries.title: Review Trigger
entries.bodyHtml:
A declared rule connecting an observation to a state change: when this discrepancy, expiry, or threshold occurs, this grant moves to this state, answered by this owner, within this clock. Triggers are the wiring between monitoring and authority, and they are what give a policy record force over a grant state.

It matters because observation without a possible transition is theater. A trigger is the smallest object that makes a dashboard part of the control system rather than a record of what already happened, and it is how policy as state acquires force over a running system.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every monitored signal names the state it can change, or is marked explicitly as informational.
Each trigger names an owner and a response clock.
Silence past the clock is treated as a governance failure, not as a pending state.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law VIII: the test of an observation is whether it can change the governing state of the system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A trigger table mapping signals to state transitions, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A monitored discrepancy producing a reconsideration record within its clock.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of monitored signals with a declared state transition, and clock breach rate.

entries.title: Correction Obligation
entries.bodyHtml:
The duty an institution takes on when it delegates consequential action: to notice, stop, reverse, and repair what the delegate does. The obligation is created by the delegation itself, not by the first incident.

It matters because delegating action also delegates the ability to be wrong at scale. Stating the obligation alongside the authority grant is what makes a shortfall in correction capacity visible before it is needed rather than during an incident.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each grant states the corrections its holder owes: which harms, notified how, reversed by whom.
Correction obligations are reviewed whenever the grant's scope or population changes.
An obligation with no funded capacity behind it is recorded as an open governance risk.
entries.genealogy: States Law IV as an object attached to the grant, so correction is authorized at the same moment as action.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A correction obligation clause on each grant, naming harms, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A scope increase blocked until the matching correction obligation was resourced.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of stated obligations without a funded capacity owner.

entries.title: Preserved Capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
An institutional capability deliberately maintained so the institution can still question, replace, or withdraw a system: retained expertise, a working manual path, independent records, a viable alternative supplier. Preserved capacities are named, owned, and funded even while idle, and they are kept honest by withdrawal rehearsal.

It matters because these are the first capacities efficiency removes. Their erosion is a governance event rather than a saving, since it is the mechanism by which a system consumes the conditions of its own contestability, destroys institutional reversibility, and ends in institutional capture.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Preserved capacities are listed with an owner and a budget line, separate from the system's own budget.
Any proposal that reduces one is reviewed as a governance change, not as an efficiency measure.
Each capacity is exercised on a cadence so that its continued existence is demonstrated.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law XII its object: the capacities an institution needs in order to question, replace, or withdraw a consequential system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A preserved capacity register with owners, budget lines, and exercise dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A cost reduction rejected or amended because it would erode a preserved capacity.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of registered capacities exercised within their declared interval.

entries.title: Corrective Standing
entries.bodyHtml:
The recognized capacity of an error-bearing party to initiate correction: to raise a challenge that must be received, answered by a named responder, judged against a stated standard, and able to change the system's state. Standing is proportional to exposure and carries procedural force rather than veto.

It matters because contestability without standing is a suggestion box. Standing is what converts the experience of harm into an event the governing system has to process, and it is operationalized by a standing mechanism.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Standing is declared per decision class rather than granted informally on request.
A challenge from someone with standing produces a dated response from a named party.
At least one successful challenge in the period changed a policy or grant, not only an outcome.
entries.genealogy: States Law VII in its Method-scoped form: exposure generates standing, and standing is procedural force, not control over the institution.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing declaration per decision class, naming who may challenge what.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge raised by an affected party that changed a grant or policy state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges answered within clock, and share producing a state change.

entries.title: Standing Mechanism
entries.bodyHtml:
The concrete apparatus that makes standing real: a register of who may challenge which decision classes, including error-bearing parties, plus the admissible evidence, the responder, the deadline, the standard of review, and the set of state transitions a successful challenge can produce.

It matters because corrective standing declared without a mechanism can be neither exercised nor audited. The mechanism is the part of contestability an auditor can inspect: named responders, real clocks, and recorded outcomes.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The register, responder, deadline, and standard of review are published, not held internally.
The set of possible outcomes includes at least one that changes system state.
Non-retaliation is attested and monitored for the parties who use the mechanism.
entries.genealogy: The mechanism side of Law VII, and the amendment surface for STD-02 where standard of review and state transitions are added.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A published standing mechanism specification with register, responder, clock, and outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge routed through the mechanism and answered by the named responder on time.
minimumEvidence.metric: Challenge volume, response-clock breach rate, and outcome distribution.

entries.title: Procedural Force
entries.bodyHtml:
The property of a challenge that obliges a response and can change a state, as distinct from a veto that stops action outright. A challenge with procedural force must be received, answered on a clock, and capable of producing a transition; it need not prevail.

It matters because the usual objection to standing is fear of veto. Procedural force is the narrower claim that keeps corrective standing workable, and it is the difference between contestability and consultation.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that determine who sets moral boundaries and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every challenge channel names what must happen on receipt and by when.
The possible outcomes are enumerated, and at least one is a state change rather than an explanation.
A challenge that is answered but produces no possible transition is recorded as consultation.
entries.genealogy: Draws the line Law VII draws: standing is procedural force, not veto, so the claim survives contact with operational reality.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A challenge specification listing obligations on receipt and enumerated outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge that did not prevail but still produced a recorded reconsideration.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges producing a recorded state transition of any kind.

entries.title: Decision Object
entries.bodyHtml:
Normative definition. A Decision Object is a versioned, inspectable record that encodes the rules, inputs, thresholds, and authority governing an operational decision.

Decision objects are first-class governance artifacts, not just logic. They must specify ownership, appealability, reversibility, and temporal obligations. Decisions that affect access, status, or rights must be backed by an active decision object.

entries.title: Binding Clock
entries.bodyHtml:
Normative definition. A Binding Clock is an enforceable timer governing system obligations once a decision enters a pending or contested state.

The clock continues to accrue regardless of internal workload, staffing constraints, or review queues unless explicitly paused under defined conditions.

Clock semantics (design-legible).

binding_clock_id: BC-010
trigger_event: decision_status == "pending_review"
start_condition: timestamp_of_trigger
pause_conditions:
  - mutual_extension_agreed
  - documented_external_dependency
pause_requires:
  approver_role: Ombuds Officer
  public_log: true
timeout_effects:
  - default_to_human_review
  - interim_access_granted
clock_visibility: user_visible

Why this matters. Without a binding clock, delay is power, silence is treated as consent, and “we’re reviewing” becomes infinite. With it, time itself becomes a governed surface and institutions pay for waiting.

entries.title: Policy as State
entries.bodyHtml:
The rule that policy is a state of the running system rather than an input consumed at deployment. A policy record has a version, assumptions, an expiry, and a current status that other objects can read and react to.

It matters because policy held as a document cannot take part in control. Only policy held as state lets an assumption going stale change an authority grant without anyone remembering to look.

entries.title: Meaningful Control
entries.bodyHtml:
The condition under which a human is part of a control system: they can see the problem, hold authority to prevent or alter the action, have time to act, have a defined path when they disagree, and face incentives that permit disagreement. Anything less is presence, not control.

It matters because oversight is the most widely claimed and least evidenced control in deployed systems. Meaningful control is tested through an intervention specification, and its absence is what turns review into rubber-stamp review.

operationalTests: Reviewers can name the state they can change and the time budget they have to change it.
Disagreement has a defined route that does not depend on personal risk appetite.
Approval rates and reversal rates are both reported, not approval rates alone.
